intro: Step down into the Basilica Cistern, a cistern in İstanbul province from the 6th century AD. Imagine a forest of 336 columns, hidden underground. This reservoir held the water of the palace quarter through a siege. And look out for two of its columns in particular: they stand on reused Medusa heads, one upside down and one on its side.
history: After the Nika revolt of 532, Justinian had this cistern built. It covers 138 by 65 metres and held close to eighty thousand cubic metres of water, fed from the Valens aqueduct and sent on to the Great Palace quarter. Then, under the Ottomans, it was forgotten. So how was it found again? In the sixteenth century it was recorded once more — only because householders were lowering buckets through their cellar floors and pulling up fish.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the 336 columns, the Medusa heads, the Column of Tears and the brick vaults above them.
facts: Did you know? Two Medusa heads serve as column bases here, one upside down and one on its side. Why were they set that way? Nobody knows; the likeliest answer is simply that they were the right height. That fits the rest of the story: the 336 columns were gathered from different buildings, so where the heights did not match, bases were raised and capitals turned over. And one last curiosity: forgotten under the Ottomans, the cistern was recorded again in the sixteenth century only because people were pulling fish up through their cellar floors.
outro: This brings our walk through the Basilica Cistern to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water. As you climb back into the daylight, remember the quiet water that once served a palace. Enjoy your visit.
